title: TFO and SYN-proxy interaction causing intermittent control-plane auth failures - diagnostic review
content:
Summary:

On 2026-08-18 23:37 UTC several Private control-plane connections from a single enterprise customer began failing TLS client auth with our control plane. Symptoms were intermittent: ~0.5-3% of control-plane RPCs returned authentication errors and connection resets. The customer reported degraded provisioning operations and occasional dashboard refresh failures.

This incident review captures the on-call diagnostic notes, hypotheses, evidence, temporary mitigations applied, and long-term action items. Root cause hypothesis (final): an on-prem middlebox (customer-managed firewall/edge appliance) was performing TCP SYN-proxying combined with kernel-level TCP Fast Open (TFO) offload and connection pooling. The interaction produced half-completed 0-RTT/TFO handshakes and re-used ephemeral TFO cookies across logical client identities, which sometimes bypassed our expected TLS handshake ordering and caused our mTLS verification layer to reject sessions (we saw mismatched session context / client certificate renegotiation failures). In short: middlebox TCP optimizations were breaking the assumptions of our control-plane TCP/TLS stack under high churn.

Why this is unusual / important:
- Private deployments expect customer-managed network appliances to be mostly transparent at TCP/TLS layer. This incident shows that some appliances do active TCP-level optimization (TFO, SYN-proxy, transparent proxying) that can change handshake ordering semantics.
- We observed failures that looked like TLS cert issues (client auth failed) but were actually caused by lower-level TCP/stack manipulation; without packet-level capture this is easy to mis-diagnose.

Timeline (key events):
- 2026-08-18 23:20 UTC: Automated SLO alert (control-plane RPC auth error rate >0.8%) triggered for customer: ORG-5582
- 23:28 UTC: On-call first triage. Error signatures: TLS client auth failures (mTLS verification error "unexpected_handshake_message"), intermittent RSTs. Customer oncall pinged; they reported recent firmware push to edge appliance 23:05 UTC (release v3.2.4).
- 23:34 UTC: Requested pcap from customer; customer pulled tcpdump at edge and forwarded a 60s capture starting 23:30:02.
- 23:50 UTC: Correlated capture with our server logs. Observed repeated attempts where TCP connection established, then client sent TLS ClientHello with 0-RTT data (TFO), server responded with SYN-ACK earlier in flow or TLS alert after partial handshake. Some flows showed client sending TFO cookie probe separate from full handshake.
- 00:12 UTC (2026-08-19): Hypothesis formed: middlebox SYN proxy + TFO offload was reusing or terminating TFO cookies improperly, causing out-of-order TLS handshake state.
- 00:35 UTC: Temporary mitigation - ask customer to disable TCP Fast Open in on-prem edge appliance (they pushed a disable via central management console).
- 01:10 UTC: Error rate dropped to baseline.

Observations / Evidence (from captures & logs):
- Packet-level notes: several flows showed initial SYN+TFO cookie exchanges that never correlated to a later ClientHello; we saw mid-stream RSTs and overlapping 0-RTT probes. In a subset, the appliance answered SYN on behalf of backend (SYN-proxy) then later re-used the same 4-tuple to multiplex another logical client at TCP level.
- Our server-side logs: mTLS verification failures with cause codes referencing unexpected handshake message and no matching client cert context. The TLS library stack (BoringSSL) logged "early_data_rejected" in some cases.
- Appliance telemetry (from customer): firmware v3.2.4 includes TFO enablement by default and an opt-in aggressive SYN-proxy optimization; release notes mention connection pooling for upstreams.
- Repro: In lab with the same appliance version we could reproduce a similar burst of failed handshakes when TFO + SYN-proxy enabled and when upstream had high connection churn.

Immediate mitigations applied:
- Customer disabled TCP Fast Open on the appliance (temporary, rolled back to previous config) — incident stopped.
- On our side, we deployed a short-lived server-side mitigation flag on control-plane that disabled Accept0RTT/early_data handling for the affected tenant to fail safe. This avoids accepting early_data and forces full handshake for new connections (patch rolled in 2 minutes).
- Increased logging for TLS handshake state and correlation IDs for next 48 hours.

Why the temporary mitigations are acceptable short term:
- Disabling TFO at appliance removes the offload optimization and restores canonical TCP handshake ordering. Customer confirmed no immediate perf regression for their user-visible traffic; their internal bench shows small latency increase sub-5ms under typical load.
- Server-side disabling of early data ensures we don't accept mis-ordered handshake data as valid; this is lower risk for security but can increase handshake latency.

Root cause analysis (detailed):
- The appliance combined two optimizations: SYN-proxy (answers SYNs on behalf of backend) and TFO cookie handling. SYN-proxy gave the appliance the ability to complete the TCP handshake locally and then establish a new connection to the backend. However, it did not correctly isolate 0-RTT/TFO cookies per logical client session and sometimes recycled cookie state across pooled connections. When our control-plane backend received what it thought was early TLS application data tied to a different client identity or missing the expected ClientHello/Certificate sequence, BoringSSL rejected or raised an unexpected_handshake_message error.
- Contributing factors: high connection churn from provisioning workloads (many short lived RPCs), new appliance firmware defaulting TFO on, and our control-plane's earlier optimization to accept 0-RTT/early_data for performance.

Post-incident actions (short and medium term):
1) Runbook update (short term) - add "If tenant reports intermittent TLS auth failures, ask customer to check for TFO or SYN-proxy in edge appliances" with specific diagnostic pcap signatures to collect (SYN with TFO option, SYN-ACK retrans without ClientHello, repeated early_data_rejected entries).
2) Client SDK suggestion - add recommended network appliance settings to Private deployment docs: explicitly disable TFO or set SYN-proxy to non-pooling mode when using mTLS with early data enabled.
3) Control-plane config toggle - make early_data acceptance configurable per-tenant with a default of "off" for new Private installs until we have hardened detection. Add an automated detector that will temporarily reject 0-RTT for a tenant showing >0.2% unexpected_handshake errors in a rolling 5min window.
4) Permanent engineering fix - harden server TLS stack handshake correlation to better detect and reject multiplexed connection anomalies earlier and avoid mis-attribution of early_data across reused connections. Target PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/agent-config/pull/482 (WIP).
5) Customer comms - coordinate a KB article and a short email template explaining the issue, why some appliances cause it, and suggested appliance settings. Include a checklist for capture collection.
6) Compatibility testing - add appliance firmware v3.x family to our integration lab and run high-churn mTLS tests with TFO/SYN-proxy permutations.

Runbook checklist (draft to be added to oncall playbook):
- On alert: capture control-plane logs around the timestamps (correlation ids).
- Ask customer if they recently updated edge firmware or pushed changes to TCP stack features.
- Request a 60s pcap from the edge appliance at time of failure; specifically capture forward/backward and show TCP options (use tcpdump -w - and include tcpdump flags -s 0 -w capture.pcap 'host <backend> and port <port>').
- Search for TFO option in SYN (tcpdump filter: 'tcp[13] & 0x02 != 0' not reliable across platforms; better to inspect options with tshark -V).
- If TFO/SYN-proxy suspected: ask customer to temporarily disable TFO and/or SYN-proxy pooling. If not possible, apply tenant-level early_data disable on our side.
- After mitigation: monitor auth-error rate for 30m and confirm reduction to baseline.

Open action items (owners and ETA):
- Maya Chen: Draft KB + tenant comms (ETA 2026-08-25).
- Diego Alvarez: Patch to add tenant toggle + detector for early_data (PR opened, ETA 2026-09-03).
- Priya Nair: Add appliance family to integration lab and build test harness (ETA 2026-09-10).
- Omar Hassan: Update runbook page and oncall checklist (ETA 2026-08-22).

Lessons learned / notes:
- Assumptions: We assumed TCP/TLS stack behavior is transparent across customer-managed appliances. This is false for some modern appliances that do aggressive connection optimization.
- Observability gap: prior to this incident our default logging did not include detailed TLS state correlation IDs early in the handshake path, making cross-correlation to pcap harder. We remedied with increased logging and the tenant toggle.
- Product implication: For Private/VPC customers we should document recommended appliance settings and consider making early_data opt-in (or automatically conservative) to avoid unexpected interoperability failures.

Appendix (useful commands and snippets):
- tcpdump snippet to spot TFO cookie (pcap inspect):
  tshark -r capture.pcap -Y 'tcp.options' -V | egrep -i "fast open|tfo|tcp options" -C 3
- BoringSSL error strings seen in logs: "early_data_rejected", "unexpected_handshake_message", "certificate_unknown" (in our case artifact of partial handshake)
- Lab repro notes: appliance model ACME-Edge-9000 fw v3.2.4, enable TFO+SYN-proxy pooling -> run 1000 short-lived gRPC connections per minute to backend with mTLS early_data -> observe ~0.7% auth failures in 10 minutes.

If you have additions or corrections, add them below. This doc will be used to update the private-deployments runbook and converted into a short KB entry for affected customers.

-- End of diagnostic review --
